item.title: Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack
item.description:
Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, filed a police report on Monday over the cyberattack that forced it to take systems offline more than a week ago.

The company said in a statement on Monday that its investigation had confirmed the suspicious activity in its IT systems was caused by “the malicious actions of others”. Until now it had described the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”.

Police and the public prosecution service (OM) urged the company to file a report last week, because a criminal investigation cannot start without one.

It is not clear why Ahold Delhaize has now decided to do so, broadcaster NOS reported.

The company did notify the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the justice ministry’s cybersecurity agency, within 24 hours of discovering the attack, as required under a new cybersecurity law that came into force on August 15.

Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online and home deliveries are expected to resume on Friday, October 23, the company said. The websites of drugstore chain Etos and drinks chain Gall & Gall, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, are available again.

Ahold Delhaize said it had so far found no evidence that sensitive data belonging to customers, staff or business partners had been taken. It declined to give further details while the investigation continues, saying they could compromise its security.

The Albert Heijn hack is one of the first major incidents since the new reporting law came into force. It covers some 8,000 organisations seen as vital to the country, from healthcare, drinking water and banks to the food sector, including supermarkets.

The problems began on Sunday, October 11, when Albert Heijn switched off part of its IT systems, halting home deliveries and work at its distribution centres and leaving empty shelves in some stores.

Security sources told NOS last week that servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey had been used in the attack. Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad that the outage was costing the company “tens of millions” of euros a day.

item.title: POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
item.description:
POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation

October 19, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Campaigners for the widows of former Japanese prisoners of war have said they will keep fighting for compensation after the Dutch government said only surviving partners would be entitled to receive their spouses’ unpaid wages.

Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk announced last Friday that the partners of civil servants and servicemen who were held captive following the invasion of Indonesia in 1942 would receive 42 months’ back pay, covering the period until the liberation in May 1945.

But Sterk said only widows who are still alive when the compensation scheme is launched on February 1 next year, all of whom are well into their nineties or older, would receive the payouts because a more extensive ruling would be “too complicated”.

The government has also cut the total size of the fund from the €50 mln announced in its last spring budget statement to €11.5 mln, on the basis that only a few hundred widows of the 40,000 men who were captured by the Japanese still survive.

The decision follows decades of campaigning for victims of the camps to be given the same treatment as Dutch government employees who were forced to work in Germany during World War II.

Moluccans

They include Moluccans who later fought on the side of the Dutch during the Indonesian liberation war and were subsequently persecuted by the independent government, prompting them to flee to the Netherlands.

Earlier this year prime minister Rob Jetten apologised to the Moluccan community for the way they were treated when they arrived in the 1950s.

Peggy Stein, of campaign group Indisch Platform 2.0, called for the ruling to be backdated to include widows who were alive when parliament approved a motion by farmers’ party leader Caroline van der Plas on the issue last April.

“That was when these people heard they were going to get their wages, but some of them have died in the meantime,” she told Dutch News.

Stein added that the cabinet appeared to have pushed through the ruling without waiting for parliament to debate the extent of the compensation scheme first.

“We still had to talk to MPs and had asked for a committee debate, but never had a reply,” she said.

“This isn’t about care or morality, it’s purely and solely about the technical settling of a case for the lowest possible cost.”

No official records

Sterk said it was “practically impossible” to compensate relatives of former camp inmates who had died because the government had no central records, but Stein said her campaign group had compiled its own list of detainees and could provide documentation showing they worked for the colonial administration.

“I have a list, but they say the SVB [Dutch social security bank] is legally not allowed to use it,” she said. “But if they have €50 million to spend, why can’t they find other parties to distribute the money who are able to work with us?”

Stein said she was not calling for the regulation to be scrapped, but it should be backdated to 2025 or 2015, when the government first acknowledged that the POWs were in its service. Prior to that it had argued that the colonial government in Indonesia was a separate entity.

Stein said the campaigners would continue to press the cabinet to compensate all victims of the Japanese occupation, including those who were no longer alive. “We have made a promise to these elderly people, we have signed a petition, and we are going to keep fighting for it,” she said.

item.title: Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase
item.description:
Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The body of a woman who went missing after taking a lift on a bike with an unknown man has been found in a suitcase in Amsterdam.

Police said the remains were discovered last Friday in the Amstel river and identified as a woman named as Hajar, who was last seen two weeks ago near the Rai conference centre.

She left in the direction of Buitenveldert on October 4 on a black ladies’ bike with a man whom police are now trying to trace.

Police would not confirm reports on AT5 that a passer-by found the suitcase containing the body on Saturday morning, or that messages were sent to local neighbourhood app groups later that day asking if people had noticed anybody acting suspiciously with a suitcase.

She is described as between 1.65m and 1.70m tall with dark curly hair and dark eyes. The day before she was last seen alive she was wearing a tiger print dress and white New Balance shoes.

Anyone who saw Hajar between October 4 and October 17 or has any information can contact police on 0900 8844, via www.politie.nl, or anonymously via 0800 7000 or at Meld Misdaad Anoniem.

item.title: How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
item.description:
Partner content

How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data

October 19, 2026

A letter from the Belastingdienst has landed on the doormat, and it might as well be written in code. At work, the team meeting that began in English has drifted into Dutch, and you’re nodding along while hoping nobody asks for your opinion. Sound familiar? We spoke with OmniForge, a tech company helping expats tackle the language barrier online.

Why the usual AI tools fall short
AI assistants promise to help with both of these challenges, but they have their limits. Firstly, many recording and transcription tools only support a handful of major languages, which leaves plenty of expats working in English by default, says Daniel G. Ríos, co-founder and CEO of OmniForge. Secondly, most of them process everything in the cloud, which is less than ideal when it comes to an employment contract, payslip or document with your BSN on it.

The risk is not theoretical. When hackers posted Odido’s customer data online, millions of people were reminded how far personal data can travel. “In the best case scenario, your data might be used to profile you for ads,” Daniel says, “but in the case of data exfiltration from cloud providers, your data might also be used for nefarious purposes.”

A local alternative, built by expats
OmniForge is a privacy-first AI desktop app for macOS and Windows that transcribes meetings and answers questions about your documents, all on your own computer. It was built by a team of expats in the Netherlands who, as Daniel puts it, “experience the exact same bilingual friction our users do.”
https://omniforge.online/dutchnews

“People should not have to compromise on their personal information in order to benefit from a service,” he says. In practice, the AI engine lives on your machine rather than in a data centre. “You could disconnect your WiFi entirely, and it will still securely transcribe your meetings and analyse your documents.” Only account login and subscription management are online.

There’s an environmental upside too, Daniel argues: running AI on your own computer’s spare processing power, what he calls “Green AI at the Edge,” can avoid the electricity and cooling water that big cloud models require from data centres.

When the meeting switches language
Language is where OmniForge stands out. It transcribes audio in 25 languages, including Dutch, English, German, French, Spanish and Polish, and can write summaries and answers in around 200 languages. In other words, a meeting held in Dutch can be summarised in whichever language you read most comfortably.

Then there’s the meeting that starts in English and slides into Dutch. Other tools make you pick a language in advance, Daniel says, whereas OmniForge listens for mid-sentence switches. He admits the transcript does not always get the spoken language right, but because the summary can be generated in any supported language regardless of the input, the gist still comes through.

A typical user, he says, is an international professional in a technical project meeting where half the team defaults to Dutch. Instead of stopping the flow to ask for translations, they record locally, having the assurance that a full English summary will be waiting the moment the meeting ends.

Decoding the paperwork
The same tool works on documents, not just audio. You can drop a Dutch PDF into OmniForge, whether it’s a letter from your landlord or your VvE, a payslip or a notice from the Belastingdienst, then ask questions and get an explanation in English.

Phone calls are covered, too. If you’re talking to the gemeente, put the phone on speaker and record the conversation: even if you feel lost during the call, OmniForge transcribes it so you have a comprehensive summary to review the moment you hang up. “It takes the stress out of local administration,” is how Daniel puts it.

Built for international teams
For employers, the same features make onboarding and internal meetings more inclusive: colleagues who are not fully fluent can follow along through a summary in their preferred language. And because OmniForge records locally, there’s no bot joining your video calls. A project manager juggling several projects can also keep a workspace for each, store meetings and documents together, and ask the assistant for recaps or highlights.

Moreover, local processing represents a win for compliance: HR handles sensitive employee data, and client confidentiality is non-negotiable. Companies are increasingly wary of staff feeding sensitive information to AI chatbots, Daniel explains. “Keeping everything in-house means GDPR compliance by default.” Many cloud tools go to great lengths to get certified, he notes, “but that just means they took steps to secure their customers’ data. With OmniForge, each customer is the sole owner of their data.”

Limitations and next steps
Daniel is upfront about OmniForge’s limits. Because everything runs on your device, transcription speed depends on your hardware: a brand-new machine will get through an hour-long meeting much faster than an older laptop. The assistant is above-average at summaries, highlights and finding information in your documents, “but it cannot compete with the likes of ChatGPT or Claude in terms of raw intelligence,” Daniel concedes, since it has a fraction of the resources.

OmniForge’s next steps will focus on speeding up the models on older hardware and adding more regional dialects. A mobile version is also planned, depending on how many people adopt the app.

Try it on your next confusing letter
The best first step, Daniel says, is to try OmniForge on your next meeting or baffling Dutch letter. Paid tiers start at €9.99 per month for unlimited quotas for individual users. But there’s a generous free tier so you can try before you buy: 40 complimentary minutes per recording and 50 indexed files. All you need to do is download OmniForge for Mac or Windows for free and register.

item.title: PM Jetten and partner expecting a baby in 2027
item.description:
PM Jetten and partner expecting a baby in 2027

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten is going to become a father next year, he announced on social media on Monday.

He and his partner, Argentinian professional hockey player Nicolás Keenan, wrote on Instagram: “Someone very special is on the way. See you in 2027, little one.”

The couple posted the message with a photo of themselves holding an ultrasound scan.

The pair also posted a picture with the baby’s surrogate mother, named as Lisa.

“There are no words big enough to thank our egg donor, our surrogate mum Lisa and both their families,” they wrote. “None of this would be possible without you.”

The message was written in Dutch, Spanish and English. A statement on the website of Jetten’s party, D66, says the surrogacy is not commercial and that Lisa and the donor, who are both Dutch, are acquaintances of Jetten and Keenan.

“I grew up in a warm and loving environment and now have a fantastic family of my own,” Lisa said in the statement. “With the unconditional support of our loved ones, surrogacy feels like a very special way to contribute to making our dear friends’ dream come true.”

item.title: England’s Dutch coach Sarina Wiegman extends contract until 2029
item.description:
England’s Dutch coach Sarina Wiegman extends contract until 2029

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch football coach Sarina Wiegman has extended her contract with the England women’s team by two years, taking her up to the 2029 European Championships.

Wiegman, 56, led the team to two European titles in 2022 and 2025, as well as their first World Cup final in 2023, when they lost to Spain.

Prior to that she won the European Championships with the Dutch national team in 2017 and reached the World Cup final two years later, losing 2-0 to the United States.

“I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football,” she said in a statement released by the English Football Association (FA).

“Working for a world-class organisation like the FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day.”

FA chief executive Mark Bullingham described Wiegman as “an incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments”. He added: “There is no one better to lead the Lionesses into the next two tournaments.”

Commentators had widely expected the Dutchwoman to leave her post after next year’s World Cup, after England failed to qualify automatically for the tournament.

A 4-0 loss to Spain in June, the team’s heaviest defeat since Wiegman took charge, means they will have to come through a play-off tournament with Greece, Ukraine and Slovakia to reach the finals in Brazil.

Wiegman said: “Anyone who knows me will understand that my main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come.

“We have an important job to do to confirm our place in Brazil, and hopefully we can do that and give the country another special summer to remember next year.”

item.title: Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation
item.description:
Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Hundreds of people missed their flights and thousands more faced long delays at Schiphol on Sunday after all 78 of the airport’s automatic passport gates went down at around 6am.

The Royal Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border checks, said the outage was caused by an IT malfunction and that there was “no indication whatsoever” of a cyberattack.

The exact cause is still being investigated, but the results will not be made public, Marechaussee head of press, Major Mike Hofman, told Dutch News.

“For operational reasons, we do not comment regarding the further configuration, operation and technical details of our systems,” he said.

With the e-gates down, everyone flying to or from a country outside the Schengen area had to be checked manually by hand, including passengers in transit. The Marechaussee opened every desk and carried out less thorough checks to keep the queues moving.

Passengers waited an hour on average, and some waited up to an hour and a half, Schiphol officials said. The gates were working again by around 3pm.

KLM held departures where possible, and Transavia said it would be flexible with rebookings. A claims specialist told the Telegraaf the number of people affected in some way could run into the tens of thousands.

Few are likely to receive compensation, experts told the paper, because the outage will probably count as force majeure since the e-gates are run by the Marechaussee, not the airlines. The Marechaussee said travellers who missed their flights should contact their airline.

The outage happened during one of the busiest weekends of the autumn, as the one-week October school holiday began in the middle and south of the country and ended in the north. The Amsterdam marathon on Sunday also attracted thousands of runners to the city from all over the world.

item.title: Police investigate Grolsch beer tasting contamination
item.description:
Police investigate Grolsch beer tasting contamination

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eleven people fell ill on Saturday afternoon after tasting water during a tour of the Grolsch brewery in Enschede. The water may have been contaminated with caustic soda, according to local broadcaster RTV Oost.

The group of nine visitors and two guides had been given shot glasses of the spring water used to brew the beer, a tasting that has been part of the tour for years.

One of the victims told RTV Oost that several people noticed a strange, sour taste and a burning feeling in their stomach after drinking it. Members of the group became nauseous and vomited, and the broadcaster said they may have suffered internal burns to the throat, oesophagus and stomach.

Several ambulances went to the brewery, and a German trauma team was called out but turned out not to be needed. All 11 were out of hospital on Sunday, and one spent the night in hospital, Grolsch told public broadcaster NOS.

Police have started a forensic investigation, and the labour inspectorate is also investigating. A police spokesperson told NOS it could have been an accident, “or something else could be going on”.

Grolsch said the tap the group drank from is separate from the rest of the production process, and that the quality and safety of its beer “are not and have not been at risk”. The company said it would not comment on possible causes while the investigation is ongoing.

item.title: Feyenoord stretch lead ahead of Eredivisie top clash against PSV
item.description:
Feyenoord stretch lead ahead of Eredivisie top clash against PSV

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord have opened up a three-point lead at the top of the Eredivisie ahead of next weekend’s clash with PSV, following the defending champions’ shock defeat at ADO Den Haag.

The Rotterdammers were made to work for their points in a seven-goal thriller at Telstar.

They took the lead after just 25 seconds when Gaoussou Diarra finished off a sweeping move and were 3-1 up after 32 minutes when Sem Steijn profited from good combination work by Gjivai Zechiël and Givairo Read.

Patrick Brouwer reduced the deficit five minutes later, but a second-half penalty by Steijn proved to be enough despite Noach Shenkman scoring a third for Telstar on 69 minutes.

Peter Bosz refused to blame the last-minute defeat at ADO on his injury crisis as he looks ahead to a testing week, with a trip to Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by the visit of Feyenoord on Sunday.

PSV looked to be on course for a routine win when Sven Mijnans put them ahead in the 21st minute. But the midfielder’s dismissal just before half-time triggered a second-half collapse that culminated in Matej Sin’s headed winner for ADO in the 93rd minute.

Mijnans, who played as a makeshift striker, will be suspended for the game against Feyenoord, while Guus Til also went off after complaining of blurred vision after landing hard on his neck in the first half and is doubtful for the next week.

But Bosz said he did not fear his team was sliding into a “tricky situation” in the absence of other senior players such as Jerdy Schouten, Ricardo Pepi and new signing Sami Ouaissa.

“This is another chance to win a game,” he said. “Stick our chests out and not think in fear.”

AZ drop points

AZ Alkmaar also dropped points against a newly promoted club as they could only draw 2-2 with Cambuur Leeuwarden even after the Friesland club lost Devid Bouah to a second yellow card early in the second half.

Twente Enschede missed the chance to leap into second place as Spanish striker Ángel Alarcón scored two superb goals for Utrecht to lift Anthony Correia’s team to 11th place.

Julian Brandt and Jorthy Mokio both scored twice as Ajax won 5-2 in Groningen in a match that saw both goalkeepers save penalties.

A double by Anthony Descotte looked to have earned Fortuna Sittard the points at NEC until Willum Thór Willumsson popped up with an injury-time header to snatch a draw for the struggling Nijmegen club.

item.title: Major infrastructure projects shelved to clear €18bn for repairs
item.description:
Major infrastructure projects shelved to clear €18bn for repairs

October 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government is shelving dozens of new road, rail and waterway projects so it can spend €18 billion on overdue and essential maintenance over the next 15 years.

Plans to extend the RandstadRail metro link between Rotterdam and The Hague, upgrade the A28 between Amersfoort and Hoogeveen and make the island of Ameland more accessible are among the 29 projects being put on hold.

Infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans, announcing the list on Friday, said the government was having to make “painful choices” in order to catch up on the backlog of repairs built up under successive governments.

Many of the Netherlands’ roads, bridges and viaducts were built between the 1950s and 1970s, but the two main maintenance programmes have been structurally underfunded for years.

Karremans told parliament he was “reprioritising” the list of planned new projects “that we have been dreaming of for years because we need to carry out essential maintenance and modernisation”.

Last year the Mobiliteitsfonds and the Deltafonds faced a shortfall of €80 billion for the period up to 2040, though this figure has been trimmed to €65 billion in the light of investments announced in the coalition agreement and next year’s budget.

Roads, railways and canals

The highways and waterways agency warned last year that an extra €34.5 billion was needed to repair tunnels, locks and bridges, while railtrack operator ProRail says it needs another €20 billion between now and 2038.

Last week the Court of Audit said another €9.5 billion needed to be spent to make motorways and railways strong enough to transport military supplies during a war.

Karremans’ redistribution will allow maintenance to be undertaken on critical infrastructure such as the pumping station at IJmuiden, which needs a €2.3 billion upgrade. The current pump, which drains an area where four million people live, was built in 1975, while the sluice dates from 1940.

Another €2.4 billion has been ringfenced for completing essential projects such as the Zuidasdok, a tunnel and motorway intersection in Amsterdam’s business district, and improving a 47km stretch of the A27 between Houten and Hooipolder.

High-speed line

On the railways, the government says €2 billion is needed for the high-speed line between Schiphol and Rotterdam, where speed limits have been imposed because 10 viaducts are in need of repair, while another €1.9 billion will be spent on introducing the European Rail Traffic Management System.

Another €635 million has been earmarked to improve connections in the so-called “Brainport” region around Eindhoven by building two platforms at Eindhoven Centraal station, a neighbouring bus station and widening roads around the city’s airport, where chip machine maker ASML is extending its campus.

Karremans has also set up a special task force known as ADIEU to bring regulations down to the “bare minimum”, which he believes can save €2 billion.

But the decision to suspend dozens of projects has come as a blow, particularly in rural areas that depend on road and rail connections.

Lelylijn funding

Ameland council said dredging the channel between the island and Holwert cost the government €3 million a year and a new route was essential to enable islanders to reach the mainland for services such as hospital care.

Nearly all projects in the northern provinces of Groningen, Friesland and Drenthe have been put on hold, although the Nedersaksenlijn, a rail route between Groningen and Enschede, is going ahead at the cost of €2 billion.

There are also fresh doubts about the viability of the Lelylijn, the long-cherished high-speed rail link between Groningen and Amsterdam.

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said on Friday that the line “forms an opportunity to connect the northern part of the country better with other areas and possibly with Germany”.

But she also admitted that the cabinet could not commit to the €15 billion annual investment for the project and other funding sources would have to be identified.
